title: Amplified Phones and Free Captioned Phones: Two Ways to Make Phone Calls Easier to Follow
subtitle: A plain-English look at louder home phones from ClearSounds and the no-cost captioned phone service the FCC describes, and how the two differ.
excerpt: If phone calls have turned into a guessing game, there are two approaches to look at: an amplified phone that makes the caller's voice louder, or a captioned phone service that shows the caller's words on a screen. Here is how each works and what each cannot do.
author: Nickel And Gadget Editors

sections.content: Phone calls are often the first place hearing loss shows up. In person, you can watch someone's face and lips. On the phone, all you have is a voice, and if it is soft, fast or crackly, you end up asking "What was that?" more than you would like. Some people stop answering altogether, which means missing calls from family, doctors and friends.

There are two tools worth knowing about. One is an amplified phone, a home phone built to make the caller's voice louder. The other is a captioned phone service, which shows the other person's words as text while you talk. They work in different ways, so it helps to know which one fits your hearing and your home.
Two ways to approach hard-to-hear calls

The ClearSounds phones featured below are landline or corded phones that make the voice louder. According to the CSC600 listing, that model offers tone control, so you can adjust how the sound comes through, along with a loud ringer and a visual ringer. Check each product page for the details of the model you are considering.

What they cannot do: an amplified phone does not show words on a screen. It only makes the voice louder. The phones below are landline or corded models, so they are not a fix for cell phone calls. The seller recommends the CSC600 for moderate to severe hearing loss. If your loss is milder, a captioned phone or a hearing aid may suit you better, and your doctor or an audiologist can help you sort that out.
Captioned phones: read what the caller says

According to the FCC, a captioned telephone shows real-time captions of the other person's side of the call, while you speak in your own voice. It is meant for people who have some hearing left and can speak, and it connects to a telephone line. The FCC describes it this way:
"a captioned telephone allows the user, on one line, to speak to the called party" (FCC, Consumer Guide: Telecommunications Relay Service)

The FCC also describes an internet version, called IP captioned telephone service, which sends captions over the internet and can be used on a smartphone or computer. HearingTracker reports that the service is free to eligible users through a federal relay fund, and that providers prefer the words "no cost" to "free." You need to register, meet the eligibility rules and have a US address. Captions cover phone calls only, not conversations in the room. Because FCC pages carry no dates, check the FCC's captioned telephone pages for current rules before you sign up.

items: How much louder it gets. Amplification is measured in decibels (dB), a unit of loudness. Compare the figures on each product page, and ask your audiologist what level suits you.
Tone control. Being able to adjust the sound can help a voice come through more clearly.
Ringer loudness and a visual ringer. Some models list a ringer level in dB, and some add a light.
Screen and buttons. Look for a large, backlit screen for reading caller ID.
Hearing aid compatibility. Look for headset or neckloop jacks (a neckloop is a cord worn around the neck that sends sound to some hearing aids). The CSC600 listing mentions both.
Monthly fees. The CSC600 and CSC600ER listings say no monthly fee or subscription. The WCSC600 page does not say, so confirm before buying.
Batteries. The CSC600ER keeps working in a power outage with 4 AAA batteries, which are not included. Rechargeable AAA batteries are sold separately.
Price, shipping and returns. Retailer listings for the CSC600 ranged by about $40, so check the final price and return policy at checkout.

sections.content: Setting it up and using it well
Check the product page for setup steps and what is in the box. As general advice, ask a family member to help you connect the phone and try it with a few test calls.

If you choose the CSC600ER, the listing says the phone auto-dials up to five pre-programmed contacts in order, retries, and plays a pre-recorded message when someone answers. Decide with your family who should be on that list. The listing also mentions remote audio monitoring, so check the product page to see what it means before you buy. It is a feature of the phone, not a monitored service run by a company.

The pendant on the CSC600ER calls only the contacts you program. It is not a 24/7 monitoring service and does not replace a medical alert system with fall detection. Its battery backup needs 4 AAA batteries, which are not included. In an emergency, call 911. If calls are hard to follow, talk with your doctor or an audiologist about a hearing check.
sections.label: Good to Know

sections.content: There is no single right answer here. An amplified phone makes the voice louder, and a captioned phone service adds text. Whichever you consider, check prices and return policies before you buy, and ask your audiologist if you are unsure which fits your hearing.
